value.overview: The Piratic Flycatcher (Legatus leucophaius) is a small to medium-sized tyrant flycatcher found from Mexico and Central America south through much of South America. It is named for its unusual nesting behavior: instead of building its own nest, it takes over the bulky woven nests of other birds, especially oropendolas and caciques. It often perches conspicuously in open woodland, forest edges, plantations, and other partly cleared habitats while watching for insects.
value.classification: The Piratic Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Legatus. It is the only species in its genus.
value.identification: This flycatcher is about 15 to 17 cm long. It has olive-brown upperparts, a grayish head, a dark eye line or mask, a pale throat, and yellowish underparts. The wings and tail are darker, with warm rufous or cinnamon tones often visible in the wings and tail. Its bill is broad at the base, typical of many insect-catching tyrant flycatchers. The species is usually identified by its contrasting head pattern, yellow belly, and habit of sitting on exposed perches.
value.rangeHabitat: The Piratic Flycatcher ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a breeding resident, occurring in suitable lowland and foothill areas in both major drainage regions, although abundance varies locally. It uses forest edges, second-growth woodland, savannas with scattered trees, plantations, gardens, river margins, and other semi-open habitats. It may occur in coffee plantations and is generally associated with trees that provide hunting perches and access to colonial bird nests.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Piratic Flycatcher is generally considered a breeding resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Some seasonal or local movements may occur, and individuals may become more noticeable during the breeding season, which begins in the dry-season months in parts of the country.
value.breeding: The Piratic Flycatcher is a nest usurper. It commonly occupies and modifies the large, hanging nests of oropendolas, caciques, and sometimes related colonial species, rather than constructing a completely independent nest. It may evict or displace the original occupants and then lay its own eggs inside the nest. Breeding activity in Costa Rica has been documented in the southwest and other lowland regions. The species usually places its nest in trees in open or semi-open habitats near suitable feeding areas.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other arthropods, including beetles, grasshoppers, ants, and flying insects. It typically hunts by making short sallies from a perch to capture prey in the air or from foliage and branches. Fruit and other small plant items may also be eaten, especially when insect prey is less available. It often forages from exposed branches along forest edges, clearings, plantations, and wooded pasture.
value.behavior: The Piratic Flycatcher is usually solitary or found in pairs, except when associated with colonial nesting birds whose nests it uses. It often sits quietly on a prominent perch and makes sudden, direct flights after prey. Individuals may defend a small area around a nest or feeding site and can be vocal and assertive near nesting colonies. Its distinctive nesting strategy allows it to reproduce without investing in the construction of a large hanging nest.

conservation.populationTrend: The species has a broad geographic range and is not currently considered globally threatened. A precise current population trend is not well established from the available information.
